definitions.explanation: An amphibian that lives both in water and on land, known for its jumping ability and croaking sound.

examples.japanese: {田|た}んぼで{蛙|かえる}が{鳴|な}いている。
examples.english: Frogs are croaking in the rice paddy.

examples.japanese: {蛙|かえる}が{池|いけ}に{飛|と}び{込|こ}んだ。
examples.english: A frog jumped into the pond.
examples.notes: This echoes Matsuo Bashō's famous haiku

examples.japanese: {子供|こども}の{頃|ころ}、よく{蛙|かえる}を{捕|つか}まえて{遊|あそ}んだ。
examples.english: When I was a child, I often played by catching frogs.

notes:
{蛙|かえる} refers to frogs in general, sometimes also including toads.

Alternative kanji: {蛙|かわず} (literary/poetic reading)

Common expressions:
- {蛙|かえる}の{子|こ}は{蛙|かえる} (like father, like son; literally "a frog's child is a frog")
- {井|い}の{中|なか}の{蛙|かわず}{大海|たいかい}を{知|し}らず (a frog in a well knows nothing of the great ocean - narrow-minded person)
- {蛙|かえる}の{合唱|がっしょう} (chorus of frogs)

Counter: {匹|ひき}

Cultural note:
{蛙|かえる} is a homophone of {帰|かえ}る (to return), so frog charms are popular as good luck items for safe returns. Matsuo Bashō's famous haiku about a frog jumping into a pond ({古池|ふるいけ}や{蛙|かわず}{飛|と}び{込|こ}む{水|みず}の{音|おと}) is one of the most well-known poems in Japanese literature.
